For the CFD simulation, the model included molten salt and air inside the tank. The inlet flow orifices were set as injection inlets, parametrized according to the discrete-phase modeling to enable variation for each tank diameter without affecting the mesh generation. A natural convection condition was applied to the external surfaces of the tank wall and roof. The heat transfer coefficient and free-stream temperature were set to 15 W/m²K and 300 K, respectively. Shell conduction boundary conditions were applied to the tank wall, with two layers: one for the Stainless Steel (SS) 347H case and the other for the thermal insulation. Shell conduction was also activated for the tank floor with five layers corresponding to the stainless-steel floor, sand, steel slip plate, clay, and concrete. The mass flow outlet boundary condition was adopted by an area at the bottom of the tank’s lateral wall. For the initialization process, a steady-state condition simulation with a pseudo-transient solution was executed to determine the initial values for the salt inflow, inlet temperature, outlet mass flow rate, inventory level, and initial temperature. 6 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 6. Mesh generation for tank of diameter of 22 m. This study evaluated a daily tank-start operation and tank-filling process. Case zero corresponds to the representative tank design with a diameter of 39.6 m, while Cases 1 to 6 correspond to tanks with diameters of 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, and 42 m, respectively (see Table 1). The selection of this operation condition for the scaled tank analysis was supported by the previous parametric analysis conducted in this project (project 38475).
